title: Go SDK: stream session checkpointing, resumable retries, and context timeout orchestration
creator: Maya Rivera
description:
Goal: implement a robust, ergonomic Go SDK pattern for long-lived stream sessions that supports checkpointing/resumption, cooperative context cancellation, and well-scoped timeouts so production clients can safely retry without double-processing or resource leaks.

Background: existing user reports indicate opaque behaviors when clients time out while a streaming session is mid-flight: partial aggregation is lost, retries sometimes replay already-processed tokens, and SDK cancellation semantics are awkward for callers that want a session-level deadline separate from per-message deadlines. Current Linear issues (see dependencies) touch similar areas but focus heavily on cancellation plumbing; this ticket proposes a pragmatic higher-level API and implementation that is distinct from low-level deadline propagation work.

Non-goals: changing server-side contract for stream resumption beyond a lightweight sequence-token checkpoint; implementing complex at-least-once exactly-once semantics across multi-model fanout.

Design summary:
- Session object: New type StreamSession encapsulates connection, a monotonic checkpoint token (string), and a small durable buffer for idempotency markers. The session has a session-level context (ctxSession) created by the caller (ctxSession := ctx) and can be given an explicit session timeout via WithSessionTimeout.
- Per-call contexts: Each Send/Recv operation accepts a per-operation context (ctxOp) and internally derives a context that mirrors the shorter deadline between ctxOp and ctxSession, with clear cancellation reasons preserved in returned errors.
- Checkpointing: SDK tracks last-acknowledged offset (checkpoint) and exposes SaveCheckpoint() and ResumeFrom(checkpoint) helpers. Checkpoint payload is intentionally opaque (string) to avoid coupling to server internals; servers accept and return checkpoint tokens as part of the stream handshake.
- Resumable retries: Retryable errors (network partitions, transient 5xx) allow the caller to call ResumeWithRetry(ctxOp) where the SDK will attempt to re-establish connection starting from the last checkpoint. Retry loop uses exponential backoff with jitter and respects ctxOp deadlines.
- Idempotency markers: For user-level operations that are not token-aligned (e.g., requesting a multi-turn evaluation), SDK can attach a short-lived idempotency key. Keys survive across resumption attempts for a bounded window (configurable TTL).
- Cancellation ergonomics: Exposed errors differentiate CancelledByCaller (ctx canceled) from DeadlineExpired (op-level deadline) and InternalRetryExhausted. Error messages include both session and op deadlines for easier debugging.

API sketch (Go):

// create session with explicit session-level timeout
session, err := client.NewStreamSession(ctx, client.StreamOpts{Model: "r-instruct-1", SessionTimeout: 30 * time.Second})
// per-message send with a shorter deadline
ctxOp, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3*time.Second)
// ensure callers can cancel individual ops without closing the session
resp, err := session.SendMessage(ctxOp, &Message{Text: "summarize"})

// checkpointing
ck, _ := session.SaveCheckpoint() // returns opaque token to persist
// on restart/resume
session2, _ := client.ResumeStreamSession(ctx, ck)

Implementation notes:
- Use a single goroutine to own the transport connection and a pair of channels for in/out. This simplifies shutdown ordering and avoids races between multiple cancels.
- Session ctx is stored independently. Callers cancel session-level ctx to signal they want the session torn down; per-op ctx cancels only the individual request/response window.
- Adopt context/err wrapping so that ctx.Err() reasons are surfaced (e.g., DeadlineExceeded -> DeadlineExpired string in SDK error).
- Backpressure: leverage a small bounded outgoing queue (default 8) and return ErrBackpressure when callers attempt to SendMessage too quickly; SDK provides TrySend which is non-blocking and a blocking Send with ctxOp.
- Resource cleanup: on ctxSession cancellation, begin a graceful drain window (configurable, default 100ms) and then force-close. This reduces lost in-flight work for clients that use session-level cancellation by mistake.

Acceptance criteria:
- Unit tests for session creation, per-op cancellation, and combined session+op cancellation scenarios.
- Integration test that simulates network flakiness and verifies ResumeFrom replays only after checkpoint and honors idempotency keys.
- API ergonomic review with SDK docs and examples in go/README.
- Benchmark: adding session wrapper must not increase 95th percentile latency by more than 5% for single-request flows compared to raw client.Send.

Open questions / trade-offs discussed in review:
- Should checkpoint tokens be cryptographically signed or opaque? (Decision: keep opaque for now; server may sign later if tamper resistance required.)
- Exactly-once semantics vs at-least-once: we accept at-least-once with idempotency markers for non-token-aligned operations; achieving true exactly-once requires server state machine changes outside SDK scope.
- Exposing TrySend vs blocking Send: UX trade-off between safety and simplicity. We include both and document guidance (use TrySend for fire-and-forget telemetry, blocking Send for core flows).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: callers misuse session-level timeouts and expect per-op guarantees. Mitigation: strong examples and clear error classifications; default session timeout is unlimited unless specified.
- Risk: long-lived idempotency keys increase memory if abused. Mitigation: TTL and soft-LRU eviction with metrics when the cache grows.

Example errors produced by the SDK (to aid debugging):
- stream: cancelled (caller) | session_deadline=2025-03-12T13:00:00Z | op_deadline=2025-03-12T12:59:58Z
- stream: deadline expired (op) | session_deadline=none | op_deadline=2025-03-12T12:59:58Z
- stream: resume failed after 3 attempts | last_checkpoint=ck_7f8a | cause=transport_unavailable

Owner notes: this approach aims to be prescriptive at the SDK layer (clear APIs, checkpoint helpers, distinct error taxonomy) while leaving heavyserver-side guarantees and global exactly-once semantics to server teams. The design should be flexible enough to adopt server-signed tokens and more advanced resume logic later without breaking consumer ergonomics.
